The speckled hummingbird (Adelomyia melanogenys) displays distinct sexual dimorphism in adult mass, with field records indicating that females reach an ultimate wet weight of 2.8 grams [Wwi = 2.8 grams], while males attain a larger adult body mass of 3.6 grams [Wwi = 3.6 grams]. This size difference is modest compared to other Andean hummingbirds but is consistent across populations studied in Ecuador and Peru. At hatching, neonates weigh just 0.4 grams [Ww0 = 0.4 grams], an extraordinarily small initial mass even by trochilid standards, reflecting the altricial state of the newly emerged chick. The incubation period for A. melanogenys, during which eggs are maintained at a developmental temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], lasts approximately 17.5 days [ab = approximately 17.5 days]; this duration is slightly prolonged relative to lowland congeners, likely an adaptation to the cooler montane environments this species inhabits.

Under the stable thermal conditions that characterize active metabolic periods in this species (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), basal metabolism was assessed through closed-system respirometry on post-absorptive individuals at rest. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded was 14.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 14.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with predictions based on body size for high-altitude hummingbirds at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively elevated metabolic scope is essential for sustaining the hovering flight needed to exploit spatially dispersed nectar resources in the understory of cloud forests. At the same body temperature, the maximum lifespan observed in a long-term banding study reached approximately 7.7 years [am = approximately 7.7 years], a remarkable longevity for a bird of this diminutive size at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Individuals were tracked across multiple breeding seasons, confirming that senescence-related mortality is minimal before the sixth year.

Reproductive phenology in Adelomyia melanogenys follows a slow pace typical of many high-elevation trochilids. Females lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a fixed clutch size that does not vary with elevation across the species' range. Breeding is tightly seasonal, with only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] produced during the rainy season when insect and nectar availability peak. This low annual reproductive output is offset by high adult survival, a life-history trade-off common among small endotherms inhabiting unpredictable montane environments. The incubation and brooding roles are exclusively maternal, and the female alone provides all parental care from egg laying through fledgling independence. At the typical core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that a female hatched in one breeding season will not attempt to reproduce until the following year, following a complete annual cycle of growth and molt.

The developmental trajectory of nestling speckled hummingbirds is rapid but structured. At 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 22 days [tx = 22 days], marking the age at which young birds achieve their first sustained flight and depart the nest. This fledging period is comparable to that of other small hummingbirds and is characterized by a steep growth curve, with chicks attaining nearly 80 percent of adult mass by day 20. Following nest departure, juveniles remain dependent on the female for provisioning for another two to three weeks. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and the development of adult plumage and song, is reached at 66 days since birth [tp = 66 days since birth] when maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity ensures that young birds are physiologically capable of breeding in their first potential season, although social constraints may delay actual reproduction.

Foraging ecology and habitat use further illuminate the life history constraints on this species. Speckled hummingbirds are generalist nectarivores that also supplement their diet with small arthropods, a protein source critical for egg formation and nestling growth. Males defend flowering territories in the understory and edge habitats of montane cloud forests between 1,500 and 2,500 meters elevation. Their hovering metabolism, already notable for its high oxygen consumption rate, imposes tight daily energy budgets: individuals must feed every 10 to 15 minutes during active hours to avoid glycogen depletion. Comparative data from related Andean hummingbirds suggest that the moderately slow life history of Adelomyia melanogenys is an adaptation to the low and unpredictable resource availability typical of its elevational niche. Population densities are low, and annual survival of adults exceeds 70 percent, a rate that underpins the demographic stability of populations despite low annual reproductive output. Future studies should examine how rising temperatures due to climate change may affect the thermal costs of hovering flight and the availability of nectar resources across the species' fragmented range.
